tool.title: Arrmanatha Nasir
tool.excerpt: Arrmanatha Christiawan Nasir (born 30 December 1971) is an Indonesian career diplomat serving as Indonesia's foreign minister since 2026. Prior to his current position, Arrmanatha served in a number of diplomatic roles, including as ambassador to France from 2019 to 2021, permanent representative to the United Nations from 2021 to 2024, and most recently, deputy foreign minister from 2024 to 2026. == Early life and education == Arrmanatha was born on 30 December 1971 in Bangkok, Thailand. Arrmanatha spent his early childhood up until primary school in the United States. Arrmanatha returned to Indonesia for middle school, where according to him he was often ridiculed by his peers as "geeky" and "arrogant" for his rudimentary Indonesian and his lack of understanding in informal Indonesian. After finishing middle school, Arrmanatha followed his parents to United Kingdom and attended Whitefield School in London, where he completed his GCSE and A Levels in 1989. He the continued his higher education at the University of Buckingham, where he acquired bachelor's degree in economics in 1993, and a Master of Business Administration from Leicester University in 1994. == Diplomatic career == After completing his education overseas, Arrmanatha immediately returned to work in Indonesia. He began his career working for Bank Danamon as an account executive from 1995 to 1996 and for Bank Dagang Negara as correspondent banking from 1996 to 1997. He was then admitted to the foreign ministry as the 23th cohort of the basic diplomatic training in 1997. Arrmanatha was put in charge of the desk for operations of UN economic and social bodies, serving until 2001. Arrmanatha received his first overseas posting at the permanent mission to the United Nations and the World Trade Organizations in Geneva sometime between late 2001 and early 2002. He was assigned to the permanent mission's second economic division, which was responsible for international trade matters, with the diplomatic rank of third [withheld]ary. tool.title: Territorial disputes in the South China Sea
tool.excerpt: On 19 March 2016, for example, Indonesian authorities tried to capture a Chinese trawler accused of illegal fishing in Indonesian waters, and arrested the Chinese crew. They were prevented from towing the boat to harbour by a Chinese coast guard vessel which reportedly "rammed" the trawler in Indonesian waters. "To prevent anything else occurring, the Indonesian authorities let go of the Chinese boat and then left toward Natuna, still with eight fishermen and the captain on board." On 21 March, Arrmanatha Nasir, a spokesman for Indonesia's Foreign Ministry, said that Indonesia still had the Chinese crew in custody, and Minister for Fisheries and Maritime Affairs Susi Pudjiastuti said that she would summon the Chinese ambassador, Xie Feng, to discuss this matter. Indonesia insists that they have the right to prosecute the Chinese trawler crew, despite Beijing's demand to release their eight fishermen. Arif Havas Oegroseno, the government official of maritime security, said that the Chinese claim of "traditional fishing grounds" was not recognised under the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. ... Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, the People's Republic of China (PRC), Taiwan (Republic of China/ROC), and Vietnam have conflicting island and maritime claims in the South China Sea. The disputes involve the islands, reefs, banks, and other features of the region, including the Spratly Islands, Paracel Islands, Scarborough Shoal, and some boundaries in the Gulf of Tonkin. The waters near the Indonesian Natuna Islands, which some regard as geographically part of the South China Sea, are disputed as well.
